Experimental Validation

The compensation results of this dissertation are simulation-based (section 9.2.2), and every quantitative heating magnitude is model-relative pending characterization of the deployed ink. The functionally graded maps of section 5.1, the chamber-keyed anisotropic-shrinkage pre-warp transform of section 5.2, and their combination (section 5.3) are predictions of a verified solver, not measurements of fused parts. This chapter specifies the experiment that decides whether those predictions survive contact with hardware. It is a plan: the experiments are lab-gated and not yet run, and nothing here adds a measured number. Its value is to state, before the fact, the exact tests and the falsifiable criteria by which each simulation claim would stand or fall, and to structure those tests so that whatever fraction of the rig is operational by the defense, the program still yields a defensible chapter.

The single decision on which the whole program rests is the choice of response variable. The primary uniformity response is not the absolute temperature spread \sigma_T of a graded part, but the paired within-geometry difference \begin{equation} \Delta\sigma_T \;=\; \sigma_T(\text{uniform}) \;-\; \sigma_T(\text{compensated}), \label{eq:val_paired} \tag{6.1} \end{equation} measured on a uniform and a compensated coupon of the same cross-section, printed in the same batch and sintered back-to-back. Pairing within geometry cancels the part-to-part nuisance variation, ink-batch drift, ambient conditions, electrode seating, and emissivity drift, that would otherwise swamp a moderate bench budget; the print batch is the blocking variable, so the design is a randomized complete block design (randomized complete block design (RCBD)). It is this pairing that makes a few dozen coupons sufficient where an absolute-\sigma_T comparison would demand far more.

The pairing is sound only if the uniform control and the compensated coupon receive the same dose. In this process they do, by construction. Dose is set by the deposited carbon-black mask, which the binder-jet printer controls deterministically: the FGM coupon carries the spatially graded mask, and its paired uniform control carries a constant-gray mask printed at the FGM mask’s spatial-mean gray level. The two masks therefore deposit the same total dopant by construction, exact up to printer repeatability. The dose-as-covariate hedge of an earlier draft is unnecessary and is dropped: matched dose is a property of the mask pair, not a regression adjustment. The one residual exposure is that the pairing now rests on the printer realizing a flat constant-gray field faithfully, which the measurement-system plan addresses with a one-time mask-realization check (section 6.6.2).

The 13.56 MHz sintering rig is not yet fully functional (section 3.2.1.1), and the program is therefore structured as three alternative execution routes of decreasing rig dependence. Tier 1 assumes a fully functioning rig and validates full-part compensation. Tier 2 assumes a partially functioning rig that can heat coupon-scale specimens but not reliably fuse full parts, and validates the physics modules rather than full-part compensation. Tier 3 assumes no working rig at all and validates the model inputs by material characterization on bench instruments. These are candidate routes, not campaigns to be run in series: the validation program runs the most capable tier that the rig availability and time budget support at the time of the campaign, and executes that one. Selecting a lower tier is a graceful fallback, not a failure, because each tier is self-contained and still yields a coherent, defensible chapter on its own.

Step 0, the impedance spectroscopy of the deployed ink (section 6.1.3), is common to all three tiers. It is the prerequisite that anchors every absolute magnitude, and it requires no sintering rig, so it is executable regardless of which tier the hardware ultimately supports.

The prerequisite to every other measurement is impedance spectroscopy of the deployed Nazdar 25 %-by-weight carbon-black/IPA ink at 13.56 MHz and 27.12 MHz. As noted in section 9.2.2, HEATR currently uses Allison’s 30 %-by-weight graphite-in-nylon data [1] as a stand-in, so all simulation magnitudes are model-relative until the real ink’s conductivity, permittivity, and percolation state are measured. Without Step 0, the program below can test trends but cannot anchor absolute magnitudes. The 13.56 MHz measurement in particular is the highest-leverage single measurement in the entire program, and section 6.4 elevates it accordingly.

The deployed ink fixes one operating point; it does not, by itself, show how the material’s electromagnetic response varies with dopant loading. Before the tiered program, a companion bench sweep therefore characterizes the bulk electromagnetic response as a function of dopant loading. Specimens are prepared at a graded series of carbon-black-in-PA12 filler fractions, spanning from below the percolation onset to well above the estimated as-printed part loading (W_{\mathrm{full}}\approx15–18 wt%). The range is set by the process, not by any literature curve: below the onset the composite is matrix-like and does not heat, and above W_{\mathrm{full}} the sweep buys headroom around the loading the printer actually deposits. The deployed Nazdar ink is 25 wt% carbon black in its IPA carrier, a distinct quantity; the saturation-to-filler mapping that connects the two is one of the things this sweep pins down. For each specimen the vector network analyzer (VNA) measures the effective conductivity \sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}(f) and relative permittivity \varepsilon_r(f) at both 13.56  and 27.12 MHz. Because the volumetric RF heating scales as Q_{\mathrm{rf}}\propto\sigma\lvert\mathbf{E}\rvert^2 (equation (4.2)), those two curves supply the per-loading material inputs that, fed to HEATR, predict the heating response and locate the loading that maximizes absorbed power for a given applicator excitation. Prior volumetric-RFAM work locates that optimum, in COMSOL, at \sigma\approx0.0425\,S/m for graphite-doped PA12 at 27.12 MHz [2, p. 1482]; the dissertation already tabulates the graphite conductivity-versus-loading envelope in table 2.1, and this sweep establishes the carbon-black analogue. Mapping conductivity, permittivity, and the derived absorbed-power estimate against loading gives the rest of the program its material inputs before any coupon is sintered: it supplies the conductivity-versus-filler curve against which the Step 0 single-point ink measurement fixes W_{\mathrm{full}}. The sweep needs no sintering rig, so like the single-point measurement above it is executable regardless of tier. It is planned setup work; no envelope values are asserted here.

Tier 1 is a part-level design of experiments executed when the rig fully sinters parts. Throughput governs its size: at roughly ten coupons per week, a defense-scale campaign must fit in about five weeks. The design is therefore power-ranked and trimmed to 53 coupons (\approx5.3 weeks), concentrating the budget on the contrasts with the largest predicted effect and deferring or dropping the sub-floor arms. The coupon ledger sums explicitly: S1a 12, S1b 18, S2 16, S3 4, and the multi-part sub-study (H5) 3, for 12+18+16+4+3 = 53 coupons. The trim order is explicit: if the budget tightens, the classification screen (S1b) drops from b=3 to b=2 blocks first; the headline FGM screen (S1a) and the shrinkage-anisotropy contrast (S2) are never touched.
